title: apply the chain rule to nested compositions of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivative at the correct input fr
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 4
2 | 0 | −3 | 3 | −1
3 | 1 | 2 | 0 | 6
Let h(x) = f(g(f(x))). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This evaluates every derivative at x = 1, but the chain rule needs f′ and g′ at the values of the inner functions.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This leaves out the innermost factor f′(1) from the chain rule for the three nested functions.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This takes the outer derivative f′ at f(1) = 2 instead of at g(f(1)) = 3, so the wrong table row is used for f′.

title: apply the chain rule to nested compositions of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivative at the correct input fr (variant 1)
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
1 | 5 | 1 | 2 | −2
2 | −1 | 4 | 3 | 6
Let h(x) = (f(g(x)))³. What is h′(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This drops the outer power-rule factor 3(f(g(x)))² and keeps only f′(g(x))·g′(x).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This omits the inner derivative g′(1) from the chain rule applied to f(g(x)).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This evaluates f′ at x = 1 instead of at g(1) = 2, so the wrong table row is used for the middle derivative.

title: apply the chain rule to nested compositions of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivative at the correct input fr (variant 2)
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
1 | 4 | −3 | 2 | 5
2 | 1 | 3 | 0 | −1
Let h(x) = f(g(x²)). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This evaluates the outer derivative f′ at x = 1 instead of at g(1) = 2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This omits the innermost derivative 2x from the chain rule for x², so the factor 2 is missing.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This evaluates g′ at g(1) = 2 instead of at x² = 1, so the middle derivative is taken at the wrong input.

title: apply the chain rule to nested compositions of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivative at the correct input fr (variant 3)
stem:
The differentiable function f has the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x)
1 | 2 | 2
2 | 3 | −1
3 | 1 | 4
Let h(x) = f(f(f(x))). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This evaluates f′ at x = 1 for all three factors, but each f′ must be taken at the value of the function inside it.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This adds the three derivatives; the chain rule multiplies the derivatives of the nested functions.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This leaves out the innermost factor f′(1), using only the two outer derivatives.

title: interpret the chain rule as a rate of change of a composite quantity, tracking sign and units.
stem: The water level in a reservoir is L(V) meters when the stored volume is V million cubic meters. At t = 3 months the volume is V(3) = 25 million cubic meters and V′(3) = −1.5 million cubic meters per month, and L′(25) = 0.4 meters per million cubic meters. Which statement about the water level at t = 3 is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The level is falling at 0.4 meters per month.
choices.rationale: This uses L′(25) alone and ignores how fast the volume is changing, so the chain-rule factor V′(3) is missing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The level is falling at 0.6 meters per month.
choices.rationale: Correct: d/dt L(V(t)) = L′(V(3))·V′(3) = (0.4)(−1.5) = −0.6 meters per month, so the level is falling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The level is falling at 0.6 meters per million cubic meters.
choices.rationale: This has the correct size but the wrong units; a rate with respect to time is in meters per month, not per volume.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The level is rising at 0.6 meters per month.
choices.rationale: This has the correct size but the wrong direction: L′(25) is positive and V′(3) is negative, so the product is negative.

title: interpret the chain rule as a rate of change of a composite quantity, tracking sign and units. (variant 1)
stem: The cost of producing q thousand units is C(q) million dollars. At t = 10 weeks, production is q(10) = 40 thousand units and is increasing at q′(10) = 3 thousand units per week, and C′(40) = 0.8 million dollars per thousand units. Which statement about the cost at t = 10 is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cost is increasing at 0.8 million dollars per week.
choices.rationale: This uses C′(40) alone and ignores how fast production is rising, so the chain-rule factor q′(10) is missing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cost is increasing at 2.4 million dollars per thousand units.
choices.rationale: This has the correct size but the wrong units; the composite rate is with respect to time, so it is in million dollars per week.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cost is increasing at about 0.27 million dollars per week.
choices.rationale: This divides C′(40) by q′(10) instead of multiplying the two rates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cost is increasing at 2.4 million dollars per week.
choices.rationale: Correct: d/dt C(q(t)) = C′(q(10))·q′(10) = (0.8)(3) = 2.4 million dollars per week.

title: interpret the chain rule as a rate of change of a composite quantity, tracking sign and units. (variant 2)
stem: The pressure on a diver is P(d) kilopascals at a depth of d meters. At t = 2 minutes the diver is at depth d(2) = 30 meters and is rising toward the surface at d′(2) = −0.5 meters per minute, and P′(30) = 10 kilopascals per meter. Which statement about the pressure at t = 2 is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pressure is decreasing at 10 kilopascals per minute.
choices.rationale: This uses P′(30) alone, treating the depth as changing by one meter per minute and ignoring d′(2).

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pressure is decreasing at 5 kilopascals per minute.
choices.rationale: Correct: d/dt P(d(t)) = P′(d(2))·d′(2) = (10)(−0.5) = −5 kilopascals per minute.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pressure is increasing at 5 kilopascals per minute.
choices.rationale: This has the correct size but the wrong direction: the depth is decreasing, so the pressure is decreasing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pressure is decreasing at 5 kilopascals per meter.
choices.rationale: This has the correct size but the wrong units; the rate with respect to time is in kilopascals per minute.

title: interpret the chain rule as a rate of change of a composite quantity, tracking sign and units. (variant 3)
stem: The number of tickets sold per week is D(p) when the price is p dollars. At t = 8 weeks the price is p(8) = 12 dollars and is falling at p′(8) = −0.5 dollars per week, and D′(12) = −30 tickets per week per dollar. Which statement about the weekly ticket sales at t = 8 is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Weekly sales are decreasing at 15 tickets per week each week.
choices.rationale: This has the correct size but the wrong direction: both D′(12) and p′(8) are negative, so their product is positive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Weekly sales are increasing at 15 tickets per week each week.
choices.rationale: Correct: d/dt D(p(t)) = D′(12)·p′(8) = (−30)(−0.5) = +15 tickets per week each week, so sales are increasing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Weekly sales are decreasing at 30 tickets per week each week.
choices.rationale: This uses D′(12) alone and ignores that the price is changing, so the factor p′(8) is missing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Weekly sales are increasing at 15 tickets per week per dollar.
choices.rationale: This has the correct size but the wrong units; the composite rate is with respect to time, not price.

title: locate points of horizontal tangency on an implicitly defined curve by setting the numerator of dy/dx to zero and substi
stem: At which points does the graph of x² + xy + y² = 12 have a horizontal tangent line?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating gives dy/dx = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y). Horizontal tangents need 2x + y = 0, so y = −2x; substituting gives 3x² = 12, x = ±2, and the points are (2, −4) and (−2, 4), where x + 2y ≠ 0.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: These are the points where the denominator x + 2y is zero, so the tangent is vertical; a horizontal tangent needs the numerator 2x + y to be zero.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: These come from setting x − y = 0 instead of 2x + y = 0, which is not the condition dy/dx = 0 for this curve.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This finds one solution but misses (−2, 4), which also lies on the curve with 2x + y = 0.

title: locate points of horizontal tangency on an implicitly defined curve by setting the numerator of dy/dx to zero and substi (variant 1)
stem: At which points does the graph of x² − xy + y² = 3 have a horizontal tangent line?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: These are the points where 2y − x = 0, so the tangent is vertical; a horizontal tangent needs 2x − y = 0.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating gives dy/dx = (y − 2x)/(2y − x). Horizontal tangents need y = 2x; substituting gives 3x² = 3, x = ±1, and the points are (1, 2) and (−1, −2), where 2y − x ≠ 0.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: These come from setting x − y = 0, which is not the condition dy/dx = 0 for this curve.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This finds one solution but misses (−1, −2), which also lies on the curve with 2x − y = 0.

title: locate points of horizontal tangency on an implicitly defined curve by setting the numerator of dy/dx to zero and substi (variant 2)
stem: At which points does the graph of 3x² + 2xy + y² = 6 have a horizontal tangent line?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: These are the points where 2x + 2y = 0, so the tangent is vertical; a horizontal tangent needs 6x + 2y = 0.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating gives dy/dx = −(3x + y)/(x + y). Horizontal tangents need y = −3x; substituting gives 6x² = 6, x = ±1, and the points are (1, −3) and (−1, 3), where x + y ≠ 0.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This finds one solution but misses (−1, 3), which also lies on the curve with 3x + y = 0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There are no points with a horizontal tangent line.
choices.rationale: Setting 3x + y = 0 and substituting into the equation gives 6x² = 6, which has real solutions, so horizontal tangents exist.

title: locate points of horizontal tangency on an implicitly defined curve by setting the numerator of dy/dx to zero and substi (variant 3)
stem: At which points does the graph of x² + y² − 4x = 0 have a horizontal tangent line?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: These are the points where y = 0, so the tangent is vertical; a horizontal tangent needs the numerator 2x − 4 to be zero.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This finds one solution but misses (2, −2), which also lies on the circle with x = 2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating gives dy/dx = (4 − 2x)/(2y) = (2 − x)/y. Horizontal tangents need x = 2; substituting gives y² = 4, so the points are (2, 2) and (2, −2), where y ≠ 0.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The point (2, 0) is the center of the circle, not a point on the graph, since 4 + 0 − 8 ≠ 0.

title: build the tangent line to an implicit curve at a point and use it to find an intercept.
stem: The point (0, 2) lies on the curve y² − xy = 4. The line tangent to the curve at (0, 2) crosses the x-axis at what value of x?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating gives 2y·y′ − y − x·y′ = 0, so y′ = y/(2y − x) = 2/4 = 1/2 at (0, 2). The tangent y = 2 + x/2 meets y = 0 at x = −4.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the slope −1/2, the negative of dy/dx, so the tangent line is reflected and crosses the axis on the wrong side.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses the normal line, with slope −2, instead of the tangent line with slope 1/2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses 2 as the slope, which is the reciprocal of dy/dx = 1/2, and so describes a different line.

title: build the tangent line to an implicit curve at a point and use it to find an intercept. (variant 1)
stem: The point (1, 2) lies on the curve x² + xy + y² = 7. The line tangent to the curve at (1, 2) crosses the x-axis at what value of x?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses the slope +4/5, the negative of dy/dx, so the line is reflected and crosses the axis on the wrong side of x = 1.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the normal line, with slope 5/4, instead of the tangent line with slope −4/5.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses −5/4 as the slope, which inverts dy/dx = −Fx/Fy to −Fy/Fx.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating gives 2x + y + (x + 2y)y′ = 0, so y′ = −(2x + y)/(x + 2y) = −4/5 at (1, 2). The tangent y − 2 = −(4/5)(x − 1) meets y = 0 at x = 7/2.

title: build the tangent line to an implicit curve at a point and use it to find an intercept. (variant 2)
stem: The point (1, 2) lies on the curve y³ + xy = 10. The line tangent to the curve at (1, 2) crosses the x-axis at what value of x?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses the slope +2/13, the negative of dy/dx, so the line is reflected and crosses the axis on the wrong side of x = 1.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the normal line, with slope 13/2, instead of the tangent line with slope −2/13.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating gives 3y²·y′ + y + x·y′ = 0, so y′ = −y/(3y² + x) = −2/13 at (1, 2). The tangent y − 2 = −(2/13)(x − 1) meets y = 0 at x = 14.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses −13/2 as the slope, which inverts dy/dx = −Fx/Fy to −Fy/Fx.

title: build the tangent line to an implicit curve at a point and use it to find an intercept. (variant 3)
stem: The point (1, 2) lies on the curve xy² + y = 6. The line tangent to the curve at (1, 2) crosses the y-axis at what value of y?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses the slope +4/5, the negative of dy/dx, so the line is reflected and the intercept is on the wrong side of y = 2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the normal line, with slope 5/4, instead of the tangent line with slope −4/5.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: Differentiating gives y² + (2xy + 1)y′ = 0, so y′ = −y²/(2xy + 1) = −4/5 at (1, 2). The tangent y − 2 = −(4/5)(x − 1) has y-intercept 2 + 4/5 = 14/5.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This computes the slope times the x-distance, −(4/5)(0 − 1), but forgets to add the y-coordinate 2 of the point.

title: differentiate a composition or product involving an inverse function, using table values of f only.
stem:
The function f is differentiable and one-to-one, with the values below. Let g = f⁻¹ and h(x) = g(2x + 1).
x | f(x) | f′(x)
1 | 3 | 4
2 | 5 | 6
3 | 8 | 7
What is h′(1)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This finds g′(3) but omits the chain-rule factor 2 from the inner function 2x + 1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This multiplies by f′(1) instead of dividing: the inverse derivative is the reciprocal 1/f′(g(3)).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This evaluates f′ at 3 instead of at g(3) = 1; the inverse derivative uses f′ at the point where f equals 3.

title: differentiate a composition or product involving an inverse function, using table values of f only. (variant 1)
stem:
The function f is differentiable and one-to-one, with the values below. Let g = f⁻¹ and h(x) = x·g(x).
x | f(x) | f′(x)
1 | 2 | 5
2 | 6 | 3
4 | 9 | 2
What is h′(6)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses f′(2) = 3 where g′(6) = 1/f′(2) belongs, treating the inverse derivative as f′ instead of its reciprocal.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This drops the product-rule term g(6) and keeps only x·g′(x).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This multiplies g(6) by g′(6) instead of applying the product rule to x·g(x).

title: differentiate a composition or product involving an inverse function, using table values of f only. (variant 2)
stem:
The function f is differentiable and one-to-one, with the values below. Let g = f⁻¹ and h(x) = (g(x))².
x | f(x) | f′(x)
1 | 3 | 4
2 | 5 | 6
What is h′(5)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This replaces g′(5) by f′(2) = 6, so the inverse derivative is not taken as a reciprocal.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This gives g′(5) alone and omits the power-rule factor 2g(5) from differentiating the square.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This keeps the factor 2 and g′(5) but omits the factor g(5) = 2 from the power rule.

title: differentiate a composition or product involving an inverse function, using table values of f only. (variant 3)
stem:
The function f is differentiable and one-to-one, with the values below. Let g = f⁻¹ and h(x) = g(x²).
x | f(x) | f′(x)
2 | 4 | 5
3 | 7 | 3
What is h′(2)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This finds g′(4) but omits the chain-rule factor 2x = 4 from the inner function x².

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This multiplies by f′(2) instead of dividing: the inverse derivative is the reciprocal 1/f′(g(4)).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This evaluates f′ at 3 instead of at g(4) = 2, so the wrong table row is used.

title: find the second derivative of an inverse function, differentiating 1/f′(x) again with respect to y.
stem: Let f(x) = x³ + x, which is one-to-one. What is (f⁻¹)″(2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This loses the minus sign: differentiating 1/f′(x) with respect to y gives −f″(x)/(f′(x))³, which is negative here.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses −f″/(f′)² and forgets that a second factor of 1/f′ comes from the chain rule through x = f⁻¹(y).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This takes 1/f″(1) as if the second derivative of the inverse were the reciprocal of the second derivative.

title: find the second derivative of an inverse function, differentiating 1/f′(x) again with respect to y. (variant 1)
stem: Let f(x) = x³ + 2x, which is one-to-one. What is (f⁻¹)″(3)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This loses the minus sign: the derivative of 1/f′(x) with respect to y is −f″/(f′)³.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses −f″/(f′)² and omits the extra factor 1/f′ that arises because x depends on y.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This is the first derivative (f⁻¹)′(3) = 1/f′(1), not the second derivative.

title: find the second derivative of an inverse function, differentiating 1/f′(x) again with respect to y. (variant 2)
stem: Let f(x) = eˣ + x, which is one-to-one. What is (f⁻¹)″(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This loses the minus sign from differentiating 1/f′(x): the second derivative of the inverse is −f″/(f′)³.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses −f″/(f′)² and forgets the extra factor 1/f′ from the chain rule through x = f⁻¹(y).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the first derivative (f⁻¹)′(1) = 1/f′(0), not the second derivative.

title: find the second derivative of an inverse function, differentiating 1/f′(x) again with respect to y. (variant 3)
stem: The function f is twice differentiable and one-to-one, with f(2) = 7, f′(2) = 4 and f″(2) = −2. What is (f⁻¹)″(7)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This loses the minus sign: the formula is (f⁻¹)″ = −f″/(f′)³, and f″(2) is itself negative, so the result is positive.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses −f″/(f′)² and forgets the extra factor 1/f′ that comes from the chain rule through x = f⁻¹(y).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the first derivative (f⁻¹)′(7) = 1/f′(2), not the second derivative.

title: differentiate an inverse trigonometric function of a reciprocal or quadratic on a restricted domain, keeping the correct
stem: For x < −1, let f(x) = cos⁻¹(1/x). What is f′(−2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: f′(x) = [−1/√(1 − 1/x²)]·(−1/x²) = 1/(x²√(1 − 1/x²)). At x = −2: 1/(4·√(3/4)) = 1/(2√3) = √3/6, which is positive because the factor −1/x² is negative and cos⁻¹ is decreasing.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This applies the simplified formula 1/(x√(x² − 1)) at x = −2; that formula holds for x > 1, and for x < −1 the correct form has |x|, so the sign is wrong.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor −1/x² from the inner function 1/x, so only the outer derivative −1/√(1 − 1/4) is evaluated.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor −1/x² and also uses the derivative of sin⁻¹ instead of the negative derivative of cos⁻¹.

title: differentiate an inverse trigonometric function of a reciprocal or quadratic on a restricted domain, keeping the correct (variant 1)
stem: For x < −1, let f(x) = sin⁻¹(1/x). What is f′(−3)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies −1/(x√(x² − 1)), which is valid only for x > 1; at x = −3 it gives the wrong sign because the correct form uses |x|.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor −1/x² and keeps only the outer derivative 1/√(1 − 1/9).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This keeps the chain factor −1/x² but leaves out the outer factor 1/√(1 − 1/x²).

title: differentiate an inverse trigonometric function of a reciprocal or quadratic on a restricted domain, keeping the correct (variant 2)
stem: For −√2 < x < 0, let f(x) = cos⁻¹(x² − 1). Which expression equals f′(x)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This simplifies √(2x² − x⁴) as x√(2 − x²), but x is negative here, so √(x²) = −x and the sign is wrong.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: f′(x) = −2x/√(1 − (x² − 1)²) = −2x/√(2x² − x⁴) = −2x/(|x|√(2 − x²)). For x < 0, |x| = −x, so f′(x) = 2/√(2 − x²), which is positive.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This drops the factor x in the denominator when simplifying but keeps the factor 2x from the chain rule, so x does not cancel.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This forgets that 1 − (x² − 1)² = 2x² − x⁴, not 1 − x²; the radicand is 2 − x² after factoring out x².

title: differentiate an inverse trigonometric function of a reciprocal or quadratic on a restricted domain, keeping the correct (variant 3)
stem: For x < −2, let f(x) = cos⁻¹(2/x). What is f′(−4)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies 2/(x√(x² − 4)), which holds for x > 2; at x = −4 the correct form has |x|, so the sign is wrong.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor −2/x² from the inner function 2/x and keeps only −1/√(1 − 1/4).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor and also uses the derivative of sin⁻¹ rather than the negative derivative of cos⁻¹.

title: find the rate of change of an angle defined by an inverse trigonometric function of a changing length, with the correct
stem: A camera is 40 meters from the base of a launch pad and films a rocket rising vertically. When the rocket is h meters high, the camera's angle of elevation is θ = tan⁻¹(h/40). At the moment h = 30 meters, the rocket is rising at 12 meters per second. How fast is θ changing at that moment?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor 1/40 from the argument h/40, so the rate of h is used as if the argument were h itself.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses only the inner derivative (12/40) and leaves out the factor 1/(1 + (h/40)²) from the arctangent derivative.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This applies the arctangent derivative to h instead of h/40, giving 12/(1 + 900) and ignoring the scale factor 40.

title: find the rate of change of an angle defined by an inverse trigonometric function of a changing length, with the correct  (variant 1)
stem: A 13-meter ladder leans against a wall. The angle θ between the ladder and the ground satisfies θ = cos⁻¹(x/13), where x is the distance in meters from the wall to the foot of the ladder. The foot slides away from the wall at 0.5 meters per second. How fast is θ changing when x = 5 meters?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This drops the minus sign from the derivative of cos⁻¹; the angle decreases as the foot slides out.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor 1/13 from the argument x/13.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This leaves out the square root and uses 1/(1 − (x/13)²) in place of 1/√(1 − (x/13)²).

title: find the rate of change of an angle defined by an inverse trigonometric function of a changing length, with the correct  (variant 2)
stem: An observer watches a plane fly horizontally at an altitude of 3 kilometers. The angle of elevation is θ = tan⁻¹(3/x), where x is the horizontal distance in kilometers from the observer to the plane. The plane is approaching at 400 kilometers per hour, so dx/dt = −400. How fast is θ changing when x = 4 kilometers?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This has the correct size but the wrong sign: the plane is approaching, so the angle of elevation is increasing.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This keeps the chain factors but drops 1/(1 + (3/x)²) = 16/25 from the arctangent derivative.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor −3/x² from the inner function 3/x, using only 1/(1 + (3/x)²)·dx/dt.

title: find the rate of change of an angle defined by an inverse trigonometric function of a changing length, with the correct  (variant 3)
stem: A kite is flown on a 100-meter string held taut at ground level. The angle θ between the string and the ground satisfies θ = sin⁻¹(h/100), where h is the kite's height in meters. The kite is rising at 2 meters per second. How fast is θ changing when h = 60 meters?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor 1/100 from the argument h/100, so dh/dt = 2 is used unscaled.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This leaves out the square root and uses 1/(1 − (h/100)²) in place of 1/√(1 − (h/100)²).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: dθ/dt = [1/√(1 − (h/100)²)]·(1/100)·dh/dt = (1/0.8)(0.02) = 0.025 radians per second.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses only the inner derivative (2/100) and leaves out the factor 1/√(1 − (h/100)²) from the arcsine derivative.

title: recognize that a variable base with a variable exponent needs logarithmic differentiation, and apply it with the product
stem: For x > 0, which expression gives the derivative of y = x³ˣ?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies the power rule as if the exponent 3x were a constant, but here both the base and the exponent depend on x.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This applies the rule for aˣ with a constant base, which gives only part of the answer; it omits the term from differentiating the base x.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This differentiates ln y = 3x·ln x as 3·(1/x), treating the factor 3x as constant and skipping the product rule.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: ln y = 3x·ln x, so y′/y = 3 ln x + 3x·(1/x) = 3(ln x + 1), and y′ = 3x³ˣ(ln x + 1). At x = 2 this is 192(ln 2 + 1), which differs from each other choice.

title: recognize that a variable base with a variable exponent needs logarithmic differentiation, and apply it with the product (variant 1)
stem: For x > 1, which expression gives the derivative of y = (ln x)ˣ?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies the power rule as if the exponent x were constant; the exponent depends on x, so logarithmic differentiation is needed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This applies the rule for aˣ with a constant base, omitting the term that comes from differentiating the base ln x.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: ln y = x·ln(ln x), so y′/y = ln(ln x) + x·[1/(x ln x)] = ln(ln x) + 1/ln x, and y′ = (ln x)ˣ[ln(ln x) + 1/ln x].

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This differentiates x·ln(ln x) but forgets to multiply the derivative 1/(x ln x) of ln(ln x) by the factor x from the product rule.

title: recognize that a variable base with a variable exponent needs logarithmic differentiation, and apply it with the product (variant 2)
stem: For all x, which expression gives the derivative of y = (x² + 1)ˣ?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies the power rule as if the exponent x were constant, which captures only the term from differentiating the base.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This applies the rule for aˣ with a constant base, omitting the term that comes from differentiating the base x² + 1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This forgets the factor x from the product rule on x·ln(x² + 1), so the second term should be x·2x/(x² + 1).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: ln y = x·ln(x² + 1), so y′/y = ln(x² + 1) + x·2x/(x² + 1), and y′ = (x² + 1)ˣ[ln(x² + 1) + 2x²/(x² + 1)].

title: recognize that a variable base with a variable exponent needs logarithmic differentiation, and apply it with the product (variant 3)
stem: For x > 0, which expression gives the derivative of y = x^(cos x)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies the power rule as if the exponent cos x were constant, which captures only the term from differentiating the base.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: ln y = cos x·ln x, so y′/y = −sin x·ln x + (cos x)/x, and y′ = x^(cos x)[−sin x·ln x + (cos x)/x].

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This applies the rule for aˣ with a constant base, omitting the term that comes from differentiating the base x.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This loses the minus sign: the derivative of cos x is −sin x, so the first term must be −sin x·ln x.

title: combine product, quotient, power and chain rules with tabulated values of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivat
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
2 | 2 | −1 | 1 | 2
4 | 0 | 5 | 6 | −3
Let h(x) = f(x)·g(x²)/x. What is h′(2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor 2x when differentiating g(x²) in the numerator.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This adds f(x)·g(x²) in the quotient-rule numerator, but the quotient rule subtracts numerator·denominator′.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This treats 1/x as a constant factor and differentiates only the product f(x)·g(x²), ignoring the derivative of 1/x.

title: combine product, quotient, power and chain rules with tabulated values of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivat (variant 1)
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
1 | 5 | 1 | 2 | 3
2 | 4 | −2 | 7 | 1
Let h(x) = g(x)/f(g(x)). What is h′(1)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the inner derivative g′(1) when differentiating f(g(x)) in the denominator.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This evaluates f′ at x = 1 instead of at g(1) = 2, so the wrong table entry is used for f′.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This divides by f(g(x)) instead of by its square, forgetting that the quotient rule has denominator squared.

title: combine product, quotient, power and chain rules with tabulated values of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivat (variant 2)
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
2 | 1 | −2 | 5 | −1
4 | 0 | 3 | 3 | 2
Let h(x) = x·f(x)·g(x²). What is h′(2)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Product rule on three factors: h′ = f·g(x²) + x·f′·g(x²) + x·f·2x·g′(x²). At x = 2: (1)(3) + 2(−2)(3) + 2(1)(4)(2) = 3 − 12 + 16 = 7.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This omits the chain-rule factor 2x when differentiating g(x²), so the last term is 2·1·2 instead of 2·1·4·2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This keeps only the term in which g(x²) is differentiated and drops the other two product-rule terms.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This evaluates g and g′ at x = 2 instead of at x² = 4, so the wrong table row is used.

title: combine product, quotient, power and chain rules with tabulated values of unspecified functions, evaluating each derivat (variant 3)
stem:
The differentiable functions f and g have the values below.
x | f(x) | f′(x) | g(x) | g′(x)
2 | 9 | 6 | 2 | −3
Let h(x) = g(x)·√(f(x)). What is h′(2)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This leaves out the factor 1/2 from the derivative of √f(x), using g·f′/√f instead of g·f′/(2√f).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This drops the product-rule term g′(2)·√f(2) and keeps only g·f′/(2√f).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This forgets the inner derivative f′(2) when differentiating √f(x), using g/(2√f) in place of g·f′/(2√f).

title: find a second derivative of a reciprocal, root, logarithm or product of an unspecified function from its first and secon
stem: The function f is twice differentiable, with f(1) = 2, f′(1) = 3 and f″(1) = −4. If h(x) = 1/f(x), what is h″(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This keeps only −f″/f² and drops the term 2(f′)²/f³ that comes from differentiating 1/f² a second time.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This changes the sign of the first term, using f″/f² + 2(f′)²/f³ instead of −f″/f² + 2(f′)²/f³.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This subtracts the second term, using −f″/f² − 2(f′)²/f³; the chain-rule term 2(f′)²/f³ is positive.

title: find a second derivative of a reciprocal, root, logarithm or product of an unspecified function from its first and secon (variant 1)
stem: The function f is twice differentiable and positive, with f(2) = 4, f′(2) = 2 and f″(2) = 1. If h(x) = √(f(x)), what is h″(2)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This keeps only f″/(2√f) and drops the term −(f′)²/(4f^(3/2)) that comes from differentiating 1/√f.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This adds the second term +(f′)²/(4f^(3/2)) instead of subtracting it; the derivative of f^(−1/2) carries a minus sign.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses f′ instead of (f′)² in the second term, forgetting the chain-rule factor f′ when differentiating f^(−1/2).

title: find a second derivative of a reciprocal, root, logarithm or product of an unspecified function from its first and secon (variant 2)
stem: The function f is twice differentiable and positive, with f(1) = 2, f′(1) = −3 and f″(1) = 5. If h(x) = ln(f(x)), what is h″(1)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This keeps only f″/f and drops the term −(f′)²/f² from differentiating f′/f with the quotient rule.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This adds (f′)² in the quotient-rule numerator, but the quotient rule subtracts f′·f′ from f″·f.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses f″ − (f′)² in the numerator without the factor f, so the first quotient-rule term f″·f is wrong.

title: find a second derivative of a reciprocal, root, logarithm or product of an unspecified function from its first and secon (variant 3)
stem: The function f is twice differentiable, with f(0) = 3, f′(0) = 1 and f″(0) = 4. If h(x) = f(x)·e^(−x), what is h″(0)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses e^(−x)(f″ + 2f′ + f), changing the sign of the middle term; each derivative of e^(−x) contributes a factor of −1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses f″ − f′ + f, forgetting the factor 2 on the middle term of the product rule applied twice.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This keeps only f″(0)·e⁰ and drops the terms from differentiating e^(−x).

title: decide the concavity of a composite function from the signs of f′, f″, g′ and g″ using h″ = f″(g)(g′)² + f′(g)g″.
stem: The functions f and g are twice differentiable on the real numbers. For all real t, f′(t) > 0 and f″(t) > 0, and for all real x, g′(x) < 0 and g″(x) > 0. Let h(x) = f(g(x)). Which statement about the graph of h is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: h is concave down on the real numbers, because g is decreasing.
choices.rationale: This confuses a decreasing inner function with concave down; concavity depends on the sign of h″, which here is positive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The concavity of h cannot be determined, because g′ < 0 and f″ > 0 have opposite signs.
choices.rationale: This drops the square: h″ contains f″(g(x))·(g′(x))², and the square makes that term positive despite g′ < 0.

choices.label: C
choices.text: h is concave up on the real numbers, because h″(x) is a sum of two positive terms.
choices.rationale: Correct: h″(x) = f″(g(x))·(g′(x))² + f′(g(x))·g″(x). The first term is positive because f″ > 0 and the square is positive; the second is positive because f′ > 0 and g″ > 0. So h″ > 0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: h is concave down on the real numbers, because the composition reverses the concavity of f when g′ < 0.
choices.rationale: This is not a valid rule; h″ = f″(g)(g′)² + f′(g)g″ is positive here, regardless of the sign of g′.

title: decide the concavity of a composite function from the signs of f′, f″, g′ and g″ using h″ = f″(g)(g′)² + f′(g)g″. (variant 1)
stem: The functions f and g are twice differentiable on the real numbers. For all real t, f′(t) < 0 and f″(t) > 0, and for all real x, g′(x) > 0 and g″(x) > 0. Let h(x) = f(g(x)). Which statement is justified by this information alone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: h is concave up on the real numbers, because f and g are both concave up.
choices.rationale: Composing two concave up functions does not guarantee concave up; the term f′(g(x))·g″(x) is negative here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: h is concave down on the real numbers, because f is decreasing.
choices.rationale: This confuses decreasing with concave down; h″ = f″(g)(g′)² + f′(g)g″ has a positive and a negative term here.

choices.label: C
choices.text: h is concave down on the real numbers, because f′(g(x))·g″(x) < 0 outweighs the other term.
choices.rationale: Nothing in the information shows that the negative term is larger in size than f″(g(x))(g′(x))² for every x.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sign of h″ cannot be determined, because the two terms of h″ can have opposite signs.
choices.rationale: Correct: h″ = f″(g)(g′)² + f′(g)g″. Here f″(g)(g′)² > 0 but f′(g)g″ < 0, so the sign of h″ depends on which term is larger, and the information does not decide that.

title: decide the concavity of a composite function from the signs of f′, f″, g′ and g″ using h″ = f″(g)(g′)² + f′(g)g″. (variant 2)
stem: The functions f and g are twice differentiable on the real numbers. For all real t, f′(t) > 0 and f″(t) < 0, and for all real x, g′(x) < 0 and g″(x) < 0. Let h(x) = f(g(x)). Which statement about the graph of h is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: h is concave up on the real numbers, because g′ and g″ are both negative.
choices.rationale: Two negative signs in g do not produce a positive h″; the terms are f″(g)(g′)² < 0 and f′(g)g″ < 0.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The concavity of h cannot be determined, because g′ < 0 and f″ < 0 have the same sign.
choices.rationale: This drops the square, so f″(g)·g′ would be positive; the actual term f″(g)(g′)² is negative because the square is positive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: h is concave up on the real numbers, because f′(g(x))·g″(x) is negative and a negative times f″ is positive.
choices.rationale: Both terms of h″ are negative, so h″ < 0; multiplying by f″ is not part of the term f′(g)g″.

choices.label: D
choices.text: h is concave down on the real numbers, because both terms of h″(x) are negative.
choices.rationale: Correct: h″(x) = f″(g(x))·(g′(x))² + f′(g(x))·g″(x). First term: (negative)(positive) < 0. Second term: (positive)(negative) < 0. So h″ < 0.

title: decide the concavity of a composite function from the signs of f′, f″, g′ and g″ using h″ = f″(g)(g′)² + f′(g)g″. (variant 3)
stem: The functions f and g are twice differentiable. At x = 1, g′(1) = −1 and g″(1) = 4, and the values f′(g(1)) = −2 and f″(g(1)) = 3 are known. Let h(x) = f(g(x)). Which statement about h at x = 1 is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: h″(1) = −11, so the graph of h is concave down at x = 1.
choices.rationale: This does not square g′(1): it uses f″(g)·g′ + f′(g)·g″ = −3 − 8 instead of f″(g)(g′)² + f′(g)g″.

choices.label: B
choices.text: h″(1) = −5, so the graph of h is concave down at x = 1.
choices.rationale: Correct: h″ = f″(g(x))·(g′(x))² + f′(g(x))·g″(x) = 3·(−1)² + (−2)(4) = 3 − 8 = −5 < 0, so h is concave down at x = 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: h″(1) = 12, so the graph of h is concave up at x = 1.
choices.rationale: This multiplies the two second derivatives, f″(g(1))·g″(1), which ignores the chain and product rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: h″(1) = 3, so the graph of h is concave up at x = 1.
choices.rationale: This keeps only f″(g(1))·(g′(1))² and drops the term f′(g(1))·g″(1) = −8.
